Testimony Neither for Nor Against LD 706: An Act Regarding Unemployment Insurance
Wednesday, March 26, 2025
Good morning Senator Tipping and Representative Roeder, and honorable members of the Labor
committee. My name is Catherine Buxton and I am a policy advocate with Maine Equal Justice. I am testifying neither for nor against LD 706. ME] has long advocated for Unemployment
Insurance, and we continue to work to increase equity and access to the program through the Peer
Workforce Navigator Project. LD 706 makes a number of important technical changes that improve
the efficiency and accessibility of the U1 system and promote greater program integrity. However,
we have some concerns about certain provisions and recommend a few improvements that we believe are missing in this omnibus effort. I enumerate a few of these in my testimony, but encourage you to peruse the attached list of proposed amendments that may remedy these concerns.
Unemployment Insurance (UI) helps laid-off workers meet their financial obligations without falling into poverty. The Federal Reserve Board said in 2023 that pandemic unemployment programs "provided the most effective dollar-for-dollar stimulus of any program to prevent the
public health crisis from causing a greater recession?" Yet today only about 27% of eligible workers
actually receive benefitsz . In light of this, any changes to the UI program must continue the Depaitment`s hard work to increase recipiency rates and ensure all eligible individuals can get
benefits when they need them.
Addressing fraud is important, but to address it effectively and without harm we must understand
fraud in context of the recent pandemic. Prior to 2020, our unemployment system faced chronic disinvestment. This system then encountered inordinate strain as it had to quickly process millions
of claims from workers laid off overnight and implement new programs with self-attestation protocols on accelerated emergency timelines. As such, much of the increased fraud activity in

marketable skills.

Maine Department of Labor
LD 706: An Act to Amend the Laws Related to Unemployment Insurance -- Omnibus Bill
To the Joint Standing Committee on Labor and Housing
Public Hearing, March 26,2025
Good morning, Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Labor. My name is Suzan Mcl<echnie, Director for the Bureau of Unemployment Compensation at the Maine Department of Labor. l'm here to testify in favor of an agency-initiated omnibus bill to change laws related to unemployment
insurance.
LD 706, An Act Regardingthe Laws Relating to Unemployment Insurance, is an agency submitted omnibus bill that contains numerous changes, some ofwhich are substantive in nature, and some are technical/errors and omissions. It proposes a series of important changes to the laws governing unemployment compensation and the operations of the Bureau of Unemployment Compensation, within the Department of Labor. These changes seek to address various issues in the administration of unemployment benefits and ensure that our systems remain fair, efficient, and up-to-date with current federal guidance.
Summary of Key Provisions:
1. 25 MRSA �6001, sub-�2.B: Facial Recognition Technology for Identity
Verification: This bill authorizes the Department and Bureau to utilize facial recognition technology for identity verification purposes. This will help streamline processes, reduce fraudulent claims, and ensure the integrity of the unemployment system.
2. 26 MRSA �1051, sub-�1 & 26 MRSA 51193, sub-�6: Unemployment Fraud
Definition and Penalties: The bill adds to the definition of "unemployment fraud" to explicitly include instances when an individual solicits another person to file a fraudulent claim on their behalf. it also expands the grounds for disqualifying an
individualfrom benefits to include solicitation of false statements or material omissions by others. Moreover, it escalates penalties in cases where a claim is filed using illegally obtained identification information, treating the first offense as a third offense, subject to the highest penalty.

26 MRSA �1051, sub-�6.C.4, & 10 & 26 MRSA �1194, sub-�10: Overpayments and
Benefit Withholding: The bill changes provisions governing overpayments owed by individuals. Specifically, it mandates that the state minimum wage, not federal minimum wage, be used to calculate the maximum amount of wages that may be withheld through garnishment from individuals who were overpaid due to misrepresentation. Additionally, overpayment recovery through benefit reductions will apply only to the principal amount owed. The bill also aligns appealtimeframes for overpayment decisions with those for non-overpayment decisions.
26 MRSA �1192, sub-�3, 6-D, 6-E, 14, 15: Eligibility for Unemployment Benefits:
In addition to an overall reorganization of the chapter on eligibility, several additional
key changes are made to the eligibility requirements for unemployment
compensation benefits:
It expands the definition of "availability for work" to require that the individual's work
availability align with their customary hours and commute prior to becoming unemployed._lt also clarifies benefit eligibility for individuals who are able and
available for fewer hours than they previously worked.
It requires that certain training programs be are subject to approval in accordance with rules adopted by the Commissioner of Labor.
It modifies the timeframe during which an individual is excused from work search requirements during a layoff and removes the requirement to stay in contact with
the employer during that period.
The bill also revises the definition of "good cause" as it relates to an individual's failure to comply with eligibility provisions and removes participation in a Reemployment Services and Eligibility Assessment (RESEA) session within the last five years from the definition of good cause.
26 MRSA �1194, sub-�2.A: Exceptions from the Eligibility Determination
Process: The bill creates new exceptions from the eligibility determination process. These include when an individual fails to perform a work search and is not under a work search waiver, fails to respond to a request for identity verification, or is unemployed due to a stoppage of work.
26 MRSA 51043, sub--�5.B, 26 MRSA �1192, sub-�6-C: Extended Benefits for
Dislocated Workers: The bill reorganizes provisions related to extended benefits for dislocated workers to reflect modern drafting standards. It also mandates that a dislocated worker must be enrolled in training approved in accordance with rules adopted by the Commissioner.

7. 26 MRSA �1197: Elimination of the Self-Employment Assistance Program: This
bill eliminates the self-employment assistance program and removes any related
cross-references.
8. Other Changes:
O 26 MRSA �1221-A, sub-�3: It updates the employer charging methodology for
employee leasing companies, interchangeably used with the term Professional Employer Organizations (PEO), to ensure they report and pay contributions under
the client company's contribution rate. Currently less than 5% of Maine employers
are represented by employer leasing companies/PEOs.
O 26 MRSA �1085, sub-�1.A.3: The bill reduces the timeframe between background
checks for bureau staff working with Federal Tax Information from every 10 years to every 5 years.
Conclusion:
The changes proposed in LD 706 are crucial for modernizing the unemployment system, improvingfraud prevention, and ensuring the accurate administration of benefits. These changes will provide more effective oversight, streamline operations, and enhance the overall fairness of the system for both claimants and employers.
On a final note: The Bureau of Unemployment Compensation functions within a federal/state partnership. Any proposed amendments to this bill will need to be vetted by USDOL to ensure they do not constitute conformity or compliance issues, which may negatively affect the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) credits Maine employers
currently receive.
Thankyou for your time and consideration. I am happy to answer any questions you may
have.

Joint Committee on Labor Maine State Legislature 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333
RE: Public Testimony on LD 706, An Act Regarding the Laws Relating to Unemployment Insurance
Dear Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Labor,
On behalf of the National Association of Professional Employer Organizations (NAPEO), I would like to thank you for the opportunity to comment on the legislation under consideration by the Committee on Labor, LD 706.
We believe it is necessary to include amending language stating that the change to unemployment insurance rates for small businesses engaged in a professional employer organization (PEO) relationship will be delayed until the start of the new tax year, January 1, 2026, to protect small businesses from unexpected costs and to account for the programmatic and technological changes necessary for compliance.
NAPEO is the voice of the PEO industry. PEOs provide human resource services to small and mid-size businesses--paying wages and taxes under the PEO's EIN, offering workers' compensation and risk management services, and providing compliance assistance with employment-related rules and regulations. In addition, many PEOs provide HR technology systems and access to 401(k) plans, health, dental, and life insurance, dependent care, and other benefits. In doing so, PEOs help businesses take care of employees by enabling them to offer Fortune 500-level benefits at an affordable cost and providing access to experienced HR professionals. PEOs also help business owners and executives save time by taking administrative and HR related tasks off their plates, allowing them to focus on the success of their businesses. PEOs have been operating in Maine for decades.
Status Quo is Working
In Maine, PEOs, or as defined in statute, "employee leasing companies," are comprehensively regulated by 32 M.R.S. Chapter 125: Employee Leasing Companies. In two sections of Maine code, 26 MRSA �1221-A, sub-�3 and 32 MRSA �14055, sub-�3, Maine codifies the ability for PEOs to use their unemployment rate while reporting at the client level. With this as the status quo, there have been no issues surrounding the way that PEOs operate in Maine. The ability to use the PEO rate has worked well for clients and worksite employees. Changing the reporting level for

unemployment insurance could be costly for small businesses, disrupt the way payroll taxes are reported for PEO clients, and have other unintended consequences.
An Appropriate Implementation Timeline to Minimize Harm
If this body deems that the status quo reporting process should be changed, NAPEO respectfully requests that, at the very least, the timeline for implementation be amended to the start of the next tax year, January 1, 2026, to minimize harm to small businesses and allow time for PEOs to make the necessary programmatic and technological changes.
Small businesses face financial and personnel costs in complying with federal and state tax rules and regulations. PEOs have professional payroll personnel on staff, which benefits many small businesses that contract with PEOs by aiding with wage-related requirements, including the timely remittance of unemployment taxes. By providing this compliance assistance, PEOs relieve their business clients of administrative burdens which, in turn, allows those businesses to focus on growth and adding jobs.
Even with PEO compliance assistance, reporting changes in the middle of a financial year could add a fiscal burden on small businesses whose SUTA rates will change with this proposed legislation. For small businesses that will see a SUTA rate increase, a mid-year adjustment may result in additional unplanned taxes owed to the state. Small businesses plan their finances well in advance, and an unforeseen tax increase could be costly for their bottom lines. We are requesting this delay in implementation to minimize any harm or unnecessary tax increases to small business clients in Maine that partner with a PEO.
Additionally, PEOs will need time to make programming and technological changes to ensure compliance with the proposed change. While every PEO operates uniquely, a change in unemployment insurance structures will have an impact on the administration of other critical services that PEOs offer their small business clients. A 90-day timeline is not feasible to make these changes and failure to extend the implementation timeline could result in a lack of compliance and disruption to the critical services PEOs offer their small business clients.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on LD 706 to ensure the PEO-client company relationship is considered appropriately and the legislation is implemented as intended without significant unintended consequences to PEOs and the Maine small business clients they partner with.
